title: Floquet engineering of spin-valley selective transport in jacutingaite
authors: Otman Bouladiane, Kamal Azaidaoui, Clarence Cortes, David Laroze, Ahmed Jellal
abstract: We study electron transport through a monolayer jacutingaite (Pt$_2$HgSe$_3$) tunnel junction in which only the barrier is irradiated by off-resonant circularly polarized light, while the leads remain undriven. In the high-frequency regime, the driven barrier reduces to an effective static Dirac Hamiltonian with a photon-dressed, valley-dependent mass term. A staggered sublattice potential $V_z$ and a substrate-induced exchange field $m_s$ provide additional tunable mass terms. Using scattering theory, we compute spin- and valley-resolved transmission and reflection, as well as the Landauer conductance. Photon dressing shifts the barrier {Dirac masses} with opposite signs in the ($\boldsymbol{K}, \boldsymbol{K}'$) valleys and induces a splitting of the propagation thresholds. The finite barrier then produces channel-dependent Fabry--Pérot-type interference through the phase $q_x^{ηs_z}L$. We find broad parameter windows with near-perfect valley filtering ($|P_v|\simeq 100\%$) and substantial spin polarization ($|P_s|\sim 70\%$). The dominant spin and valley polarizations can be switched by tuning the drive amplitude $A_0$, $V_z$, and~$m_s$.
summary: This work demonstrates how off-resonant light irradiation (Floquet engineering) can induce a valley-dependent effective mass in a jacutingaite tunnel junction. By analyzing spin- and valley-resolved transport, the authors show that the junction acts as a tunable opto-spintronic element capable of achieving high levels of spin and valley polarization. This control is achieved by engineering the effective Hamiltonian using external fields and the driving light.
main_problem: The study investigates how to achieve highly selective electron transport based on spin and valley degrees of freedom in a two-dimensional material junction.
main_result: The system can exhibit near-perfect valley filtering and substantial spin polarization by tuning external fields and light-matter interactions. The spin and valley polarizations can be independently switched by controlling the drive amplitude, sublattice potential, and exchange field.
method: The analysis employs scattering theory applied to an effective static Dirac Hamiltonian derived from the high-frequency limit of Floquet engineering.
model_or_system: The physical system is a monolayer jacutingaite tunnel junction ($	ext{Pt}_2	ext{HgSe}_3$) where the barrier is irradiated by off-resonant circularly polarized light. The low-energy theory is based on a Dirac-Weyl Hamiltonian incorporating intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, which is modified by the photon dressing effect.
key_observables: Spin polarization ($P_s$), valley polarization ($P_v$), spin- and valley-resolved transmission/reflection, and Landauer conductance.
important_parameters: Drive amplitude ($A_0$), staggered sublattice potential ($V_z$), substrate-induced exchange field ($m_s$), and barrier width ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the high-frequency limit (off-resonant driving) and models the junction as having an undriven source/drain connected to a driven barrier region.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of conductance ($G_{\eta s z}$) on barrier width ($L$) showing Fabry-Pérot oscillations, and density plots showing the tunability of $P_s$ and $P_v$ across parameter space.
paper_structure: The paper develops the effective Hamiltonian via high-frequency expansion, uses scattering theory to calculate transport coefficients, and then analyzes how tuning $A_0$, $V_z$, and $m_s$ controls the resulting spin and valley polarizations.
why_interesting: The use of Floquet engineering to engineer topological properties (mass terms) in a solid-state system is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics, providing a mechanism to control quantum states using light.
